An usher is a person whose role is to guide, direct, or escort other people — usually at a formal event, an official venue, or an institution. They are not in charge of the event itself. Their specific job is to manage the movement and positioning of people, so that everything proceeds in an orderly, smooth way.

Think of an usher as a human guide for a space. Wherever a group of people need to be directed — to the right seat, the right door, the right row — an usher is the one who makes that happen.
The different situations where this word is used

At theaters, cinemas, and concert halls

This is the most common, everyday meaning. An usher at a theater or cinema is a staff member who helps audience members find their assigned seats. They stand at the entrance or walk through the aisles, check tickets, point people to the right row, and sometimes hand out programs. If you've ever walked into a large concert hall and had someone walk you to your exact seat, that person was an usher.

At weddings

Ushers at a wedding are usually male friends or relatives of the bride or groom (though not always). As guests arrive at the ceremony, the ushers greet them, escort them down the aisle, and seat them. In many Western weddings, there is even a tradition of ushers directing the bride's guests to one side of the room and the groom's guests to the other. Wedding ushers are typically considered part of the wedding party — the inner circle of people helping to organize and run the event. They often hand out order-of-service booklets too.

In official and ceremonial settings

In formal institutions — like parliaments, royal courts, or state ceremonies — an usher is an officer who manages proceedings, controls access to certain areas, and upholds order and decorum. These ushers carry more authority than event ushers. A well-known example is the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod (often just called "Black Rod") in the UK Parliament — an official who has a ceremonial role in events like the State Opening of Parliament. At this level, the usher is not just a seat-guide; they are a dignified officer of the institution itself.

In courtrooms

In British and Irish courts especially, a court usher is an official who assists in the day-to-day running of a courtroom. Their duties include calling out the names of cases to signal they are about to begin, asking everyone to rise when the judge enters the room, swearing in witnesses (by handing them a holy book and administering the oath), and generally keeping the proceedings moving in the right order. The court usher essentially acts as the judge's logistical right-hand, ensuring that the courtroom functions properly from a procedural standpoint.
The thread that connects all meanings

Across every single context — theater, wedding, parliament, courtroom — the word usher always describes someone who is:

  • A guide, not a decision-maker.
  • A facilitator of order and movement, not the main authority.
  • In service to the event or institution they are part of.

An usher never runs the show. They simply make sure the people involved in it get to the right place, at the right time, in the right way.

Historically, ushers were assumed to be male, and a separate word — usherette — was used for women doing the same job, particularly in cinemas. However, usherette is now considered old-fashioned and is rarely used today. The word usher is now fully gender-neutral and applies to anyone in the role, regardless of gender.
A note on an old, rare meaning

In older usage — particularly in British schools during past centuries — the word usher was sometimes used to mean an assistant teacher or a junior teacher who helped the head teacher manage students. This meaning is largely archaic today and you are very unlikely to encounter it in modern writing or speech, but it follows the same logic: a helper who manages people on behalf of a higher authority.
